# Preface
Welcome to my individual coding project! On this page I propose to explore the extent to which 2D keypoints on labeled images can predict and distinguish between different biological orders, and what body proportions carry these distinctions.

# Project proposal
In wildlife photos, animals are often occluded behind the scenery, with varying viewpoints and light conditions. Photos are often not complete and it may be difficult to detect animals accurately based on datapoints alone. Accurately detecting the species of an animal in a photo is important for many applications, such as wildlife monitoring and conservation.

## Dataset
My project proposal involves the AP-10K dataset, proposed by Yu et al. (2021). This dataset has 10,015 labeled images (13,028 animal instances) covering 54 mammal species in 23 families, organized by family and species. Each data instance gets annotated with 17 keypoints: eyes, nose, neck, tail root, shoulders, elbows, hips, knees and four paws. The authors state that generalization of models trained specific species in the dataset drop correlating to biological distance.

I want to research **to what extent proportions between 2D keypoints on labeled images can predict and distinct between different biological orders, and what body proportions carry these distinctions**. I plan to do this using a data preprocessing pipeline followed by a deep-learning model. I will need to first gather data on the dataset to find what keypoints are often included and excluded, as not all 17 keypoints are included for every datapoint.

## Data preprocessing
My proposal for the data preprocessing pipeline is as follows:

1. Filtering the data to handle missing keypoints and drop datapoints with less than N keypoints or with certain high-importance keypoints missing. The exact details of this still needs to be deducted from the statistical analysis of the data 
2. Normalizing the data by orienting all animals to the right.
3. Drop unneeded data, such as bounding boxes and pixel positions
4. Create extra features, such as log ratios between segments. Pool keypoints into groups and limbs.
5. Split data into k-fold cross validation folds

## Models to be used
I plan to test the following models for classification of the data. More models may be added later, but these are the initial ones I plan to use based on initial research:

1. Majority class used as baseline
2. Class-weighted logistic regression
3. Gradient-boosted trees

From a simple initial analysis, there seemed to be class imbalance (largest order in images is Carnivora). The majority class baseline will allow us to compare further models against a baseline. 

# References
Yu, H., Xu, Y., Zhang, J., Zhao, W., Guan, Z., & Tao, D. (2021, August 28). _AP-10K: A Benchmark for Animal Pose Estimation in the Wild_. arXiv.org. <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12617">https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12617</a>
